To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the plume of a large automotive paint shop emits large amounts of NMTHC, NO/sub x/ and O/sub 3/ and that these plume emissions are transported downwind at least 11 miles.

the ambient air downwind of the GM assembly plant contains elevated concentrations of nonmethane hydrocarbons (2 to 2 1/2 times background), ozone (10 to 15 ppb above background), and NO/sub x/ (5 to 15 ppM above background) during normal plant operations.
the plume from GM's Janesville plant contained high levels of NMTHC and NO/sub x/ and that these pollutants were transported downwind from the plant.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the measurement and modeling of ambient hydrocarbon and ozone levels downwind of a major automotive painting plant, with a view toward understanding the effects of solvent emissions on ambient ozone concentrations.
the study of atmospheric reactions of volatile organic compounds, particularly those emitted from motor vehicles and other sources, and their role in the production of tropospheric ozone.
the development of a new generation of low cost, high performance sensors for the detection and identification of chemical and biological agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the emissions from this automotive plant were of sufficient magnitude that they had a significant influence on the air quality of a region 20 miles downwind.
the plant is an important source of ambient hydrocarbon pollution in the Janesville area.
the emissions were of sufficient quantity and quality that the plume had a significant effect on ambient air quality in the immediate area of the plant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we were able to demonstrate that a large automobile assembly plant, which is a significant source of air pollution in the Janesville, Wisconsin, area, is emitting significant quantities of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides.
we have demonstrated that the emissions of the GM Janesville plant are a significant contributor to ambient hydrocarbon and ozone concentrations in the Janesville area.
we have shown that a large automotive paint plant can be a major source of hydrocarbon and ozone pollution in the area downwind of the plant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emissions from automotive paint operations can be significant and can contribute to the formation of ozone.
the ambient hydrocarbons in this plume are primarily organic solvents, which are the most common type of VOC emitted from industrial processes.
the emissions from automotive painting operations can have a substantial impact on the air quality in the vicinity of the plant and can be transported for considerable distances downwind.
